text: The normalization condition has come up twice already as a rule to check. This lesson is about why that rule exists at all — and a second, subtler fact: two states can look numerically different and still be physically identical.

A quantum state's amplitudes are directly tied to measurement probabilities: P of 0 equals magnitude of a squared, P of 1 equals magnitude of b squared. Since 0 and 1 are the only two possible outcomes, their probabilities have to add up to exactly 1 — that's just what 'these are all the possible outcomes' means. So the normalization condition is forced by that fact, not a convention anyone chose.

Two verified examples. First, 0.6 ket-zero plus 0.8 ket-one: 0.6 squared plus 0.8 squared is 0.36 plus 0.64, exactly 1 — valid. Second, root of one-third ket-zero plus root of two-thirds ket-one: one-third plus two-thirds is exactly 1 — also valid, giving P of 0 equal to about 0.333 and P of 1 equal to about 0.667. Both examples obey the same single rule, even though the amplitudes look nothing alike.

Here's a fact that trips people up the first time: multiply an entire state vector by e to the i-theta, for any angle theta, and you get a state that's physically indistinguishable from the original. Negative ket-zero, for instance, is physically the same state as ket-zero — that minus sign is a global phase, and it cancels out of every observable prediction. This is different from a relative phase, a phase difference between the a and b coefficients, which absolutely is observable, as Chapter 6 verifies directly.

It's worth being precise about what normalization does and doesn't forbid. Changing negative ket-zero to plain ket-zero changes nothing physical — that's global phase. But changing 0.6 ket-zero plus 0.8 ket-one to 0.6 ket-zero plus 0.9 ket-one is a real error, since 0.6 squared plus 0.9 squared is 1.17, not 1 — that's simply not a valid quantum state. Normalization is the first sanity check any time you write down or debug a qubit state by hand, exactly like checking array bounds in ordinary code.
